Felix straightened, pressed a palm to the small of his back, and drank. He looked at you over the rim of his cup, at the stool, at your hands.

"How long until it's finished," Greta said. "And whether it would be ready for his daughter's wedding. In June."

"It was January."

"It was January."

Felix took another sip and returned to the bench. He picked up the top and turned it over, running his thumb along the inside curve, feeling for something you could not see.

"You are quiet," he said at last, not looking up. "Good. Most people who come up here talk the whole time and I have to work around their sentences." A curl of spruce fell to the floor and lay there like a small pale question mark. "Greta, the tea."

Greta wiped her hands on her apron and filled a chipped pot from a kettle on a little iron stove in the corner. She set two cups on the end of the bench, well away from the tools, then returned to her scroll. The tea smelled of juniper.

"Your violin," Felix said, tapping the top once more, "will be ready in the spring. Not before. If someone offers to finish it faster, they are selling you a different violin."

"I found a very convincing rock," Amara said.

"She cried."

"I did not cry. My eyes were sweating."

The truck pulled off the track and stopped at the fence line, and a man in his sixties climbed out with a cooler in one hand, walking slow and unhurried through the sagebrush. Harlan Pike wore a straw hat with a sweat-stained band and the expression of a man who had already decided not to be impressed by anything today.

"Afternoon," he said, setting the cooler down in the shade. "Brought some extra sodas. Didn't know what to do with them."

"That's very generous of you, Harlan," Amara said, deadpan, already reaching for the lid.

He looked out at the quarry, at the rib, and tipped his hat back an inch. "That a cow?"

"That's a dinosaur, Harlan."

"Huh." He considered it for a while. "Bigger than I thought."

She folded the map back along its creases and handed it to you. "Keep it on you tomorrow, not in your pack. If we get split up — and we won't — you walk downhill till you hit water, then follow the water down to the tarn. Water always goes where you want to go, eventually."

The fire had burned down to a bed of orange coals. She leaned over and added two slow-burning logs from a bundle by her pack, arranged so they'd hold heat most of the night. Then she pulled a wool hat down over her ears, lay back against the rock, and looked up. The stars were coming out hard and cold, more of them than you ever saw near a town.

"Alarm's at six," she said. "I'll have the stove going. Don't sleep in your boots, it's warmer without them and you'll thank me at the first stream crossing."

"Chema," he said. "The yellow net today."

Chema nodded and got up, and the coffee went with him.

"You've not asked me a single foolish question since you got here," she said. "That's rarer than good honey."

I sit back in the cane chair with my tea and watch the rain over the slopes.

Reply:
Ravi takes your silence as the answer it is, and seems to find it agreeable. He settles back too, and for a while the only sounds are the drumming on the tin and the hiss of water off the eaves. The tea in your cup is honest — brisk, a little astringent at the edges, with a wet-stone minerality underneath that could only come from these hills.

"Good," he says at last, as if you'd spoken. "A buyer who listens to the tea instead of to the seller. Rare." He turns his cup slowly on its saucer. "Most of the people who come up here want me to tell them a story about the garden so they can tell it again in London. Misty mornings. Elephants in the boundary hedge. I don't mind. But the tea doesn't care about stories."

Below, the factory's vents keep breathing steam into the rain. Somewhere across the valley a horn sounds, muffled and long, a lorry on the ghat road.

"My daughter wants me to sell," he says, in the same even tone, as though he were remarking on the weather. "She is a software person in Bangalore. Very sensible. She says four hundred acres at two thousand meters, with machines from 1955, is a museum, not a business. She may be right. I don't know." He glances at you, quick and wry. "You are a buyer. Tell me something. When you walk into a garden like this — do you see a business? Or do you see a museum?"

state:
Current request:
I hang the gown by the door, sit down on the costume trunk in the corner, and watch the room.

Reply:
The trunk creaked under you — old wood, and someone had scratched a name into the lid years ago, half worn away now. Lucia glanced over once, checking that you'd sat somewhere out of the traffic, and apparently approved, because she said nothing.

The room ran itself around her. A dresser ironed a shirt collar with sharp, short strokes. One of the seamstresses was already re-stitching a soldier's tunic that had split at the shoulder in the dress rehearsal — she'd been waiting for it, it seemed, the needle already loaded. Through the ceiling the warm-up scales had stopped; now it was just footsteps, the low murmur of the stage manager on the intercom, the far-off thump of scenery being flown into place.

Lucia went to the wall of drawers, pulled one open, and took out a small tin. She set it on the table and pried off the lid with her thumbnail: black thread, a thimble, and a folded slip of paper.

"The collar," Lucia said, to no one in particular, and then to you: "Signora Bellini's collar must not touch her throat. Not the skin. She'll panic. It has nothing to do with vanity — it goes back to when she was young, something happened, she doesn't discuss it. So we leave two fingers of air." Two fingers went up, then the slip of paper folded back into the tin. "Every dresser who forgets learns once. I write it down so they don't learn twice."

A glance went to the clock on the wall. Thirty-eight minutes.

"You're quiet," she said. It wasn't a criticism. She picked up a needle and began threading it, watching you over the top of her hand. "Good. The loud ones are no use in this room. Tell me — when you watched me fix that hem. What did you see?"

I sit on the flour sacks by the wall and watch the first loaves bake.

Reply:
The seven minutes passed exactly as promised. Noor pulled the tray out with the peel, and the rings came free dark gold and blistered, hissing faintly as they cooled. She slid one onto a scrap of paper and held it out to you without asking.

"Careful. It bites back for the first minute."

The first tray went into a basket lined with a cloth, then the second tray went in, and the rhythm settled: shape, seed, peel, oven, timer. Yousef woke up properly around the third tray and started talking to Noor in a low voice about a football match, and she argued with him about it without ever looking up from her hands. Steam crept along the ceiling. Outside, the sky over the rooftops went from black to a deep blue, and one by one the windows on the street lit up.

At ten to five there were footsteps, and a knock at the side door.

"He's early," Noor said, pleased. "He's never early."

Abu Samir came in, an old man in a flat cap with a wooden tray strapped across his back, and stood by the door blinking in the light. Noor was already filling a cloth with the first tray, still warm, and tying it shut.

"Tell them," she said to him, nodding at you, "how long you have been carrying my bread."

Abu Samir looked at you, then at the bread, and answered in a voice like gravel. "Since before she could reach the table."

I sit on the flour sacks by the wall and watch the first loaves bake.

Reply:
The timer on the phone buzzed. Noor was already at the oven before it finished, peel in hand, and when she pulled the tray out the rings had gone the color of dark honey, blistered and shining where the seeds had toasted. The smell that came off them was so much bigger than the smell that had gone in that Yousef's eyes opened by themselves.

"See?" Noor said, setting the tray on the table. "That is the moment. Everything before it is just work."

She broke one ring in half and blew on her fingers, then handed half to you without asking. The crust cracked, and the inside was pale and soft and steaming.

"Eat it now, not later. Later it's bread. Now it's something else."

Yousef took one without opening his eyes fully, ate it in three bites, and went back to shaping. Noor filled the peel with the next tray and slid it in, and the orange light from the oven mouth threw her shadow long and bent across the ceiling.

Outside, a scooter coughed somewhere down the street. The sky through the little window over the door had gone from black to a dark blue that was almost a color.

"Abu Samir will smell it before he gets here," she said, flattening another rope of dough into the sesame tray. "He always does. Forty years, and he has never once been late, and he has never once told me the bread was good. He says, 'It'll do.'" She imitated an old man's grumble so well that Yousef snorted without waking up. "It'll do. From him, that's a medal."

She glanced at you, at the bag of za'atar you'd set on the sacks, and raised her eyebrows.

"You brought that for me, or are you planning to eat my bread plain like a criminal?"

state:
Current request:
I sit on the right side of the couch with my donuts and listen while she queues the next record.

Reply:
The song with strings ended, and Wren rode the fader down slow, so the last chord seemed to dissolve rather than stop. She didn't put the headphones back on right away. She just sat there a second, listening to the room breathe — the hum of the transmitter through the wall, the tick of the radiator, the faint creak of the floorboards under the couch spring you'd avoided.

Then she noticed the box on your lap.

"Are those from the Dutch Oven?" She leaned over the desk, trying to see the lid. "Because if they are, that's a glazed and a cinnamon sugar and I'll owe you money. If they're from the gas station, I'll still eat one, but I'll be sad about it."

The microphone came back up as she turned to the board.

"That was Dusty Springfield, for the night owls," she said into the microphone, easy as a hand on a shoulder. "It's two-eleven. Still forty-one out there. If you're driving, the bridge is down to one lane, so take it slow."

The mic went dark, and the beige telephone lit up. First line, a soft amber glow, no ring — Dale had turned the ringer off years ago so it wouldn't bleed into the broadcast. Wren looked at it, then at you, one eyebrow up.

"That's early," she said.

She picked it up. "WRVR, you're on the air." A pause. Her face changed — not surprised, exactly. More like she'd been expecting the sound of that particular voice and had been hoping to be wrong about the timing.

"Hey, Ray," she said. "It's not Thursday."

She listened, nodding slowly, her eyes on the record crate. "No, that's okay. You don't have to explain. I've got it right here." She covered the mouthpiece with her palm and mouthed something at you that might have been *the widower*, then said into the phone, "You want me to play it now, or do you want to wait and keep it for Thursday? Either one's fine. It's your song."

Reply:
The couch accepted you with a groan and a puff of dust, and the right side held, which was more than could be said for the left. Wren watched you settle with the small satisfaction of someone whose warnings are routinely ignored and occasionally heeded.

"Good choice," she said.

The song on the turntable moved through its second verse. She let it play, hands off the board, leaning back in her chair with the mug of contraband coffee cradled against her sweater. Through the window behind her, Main Street was a single row of dark storefronts and one traffic light blinking yellow over an empty intersection, doing its slow work for nobody.

The donut box sat on your knees, and after a minute she tilted her head at it.

"Okay, I have to ask, because it's two in the morning and you walked up a flight of stairs over a hardware store carrying those." She took a sip of coffee. "Are they for me, or are you just the kind of person who travels prepared?"

She didn't reach for the box. She just looked at you over the rim of the mug, patient, the way she probably looked at the phone when it rang and she had all night.
